title: How Maid In T.O. built a call flow that keeps callers on the line
summary: A Toronto cleaning company watched where callers hung up, then changed its call flow, and what Sona asks, to keep them talking.
body_markdown:
Sidrah Hassan remembers the night someone on her cleaning team was locked out of an after-hours commercial job. The team had no choice but to call the customer for access to the property. When the customer called back, the phone system did just what it was set up to do: it sent the call to voicemail. That was when Sidrah realized urgent after-hours calls should ring her first.


“We were all over the place,” Sidrah said. She owns Maid In T.O., a residential and commercial cleaning company in Toronto. Before moving to Quo, the team spent 10 of its 11 years in business getting by on a basic virtual phone system, a separate texting service, WhatsApp, and Burner. When the office manager was out and Sidrah took over the calls, the whole setup had to be switched over by hand.


“It was just a lot of manual juggling and a lot of different systems which we were trying to piece together,” she said.


Since the switch, the team has kept adjusting its call flow based on where callers drop off. Here’s how they fixed their phone menu, after-hours call flow, and the questions Sona asks, with steps you can copy.


##


**Give callers a clear path**


Maid In T.O.’s business hours run 8:30 a.m. to 5 p.m. ET. In that window, callers hear a phone menu: press 1 for a new booking, 2 for an existing booking, or 3 to reach what the company calls its customer happiness team. The team recorded its own greeting for each option.


The menu used to stop at three options. Some callers hung up before choosing a number, so the team added a fourth route that needs no keypress. If callers press nothing, the call rings the office manager directly. Even more calls started getting through, and that route now sees “quite a bit” of traffic.


Sidrah doesn’t blame callers who press nothing. “If they miss every single option, they weren’t paying attention,” she said. “I know it happens. It happens to me, too.”


### **How to set up a phone menu in Quo:**


1. In **Settings** , go to **Phone numbers** .
2. Select the number you want to add a phone menu to.
3. Turn on **Enable business hours** , then set your time zone and schedule. Under **Call flow** , click **Edit call flow** to open the call flow builder.
4. Drag the **Phone menu** step onto the **During hours** path of your **Business hours** condition.
5. Click **Add greeting message** , then upload an audio file, record one, or use text-to-speech.
6. Click **Add keypad option** for each choice you want callers to have.
7. Include a voice-triggered keyword option that callers can say to select a specific menu option.
8. Give each option a destination, such as **Ring users** , **Voicemail** , or **Sona.** You can’t publish if an option has no next step.
9. Under **No selection** , switch the default (voicemail) to **Ring users** and pick a person on your team, so callers who press nothing still reach someone. Alternatively, add a keypad option such as 0 for “speak to someone” and say so in your greeting.
10. Click **Publish** . Changes aren’t live until you do. Then call your number from another phone to hear what callers hear.


Note: Phone menus are available on the Business and Scale plans.


To draft changes without touching your live setup, click **+ Create new call flow** , add a name and emoji, and build it. Publishing replaces your live flow, so publish when you’re ready, or click the arrow next to **Publish now** and choose **Schedule to publish later** . Schedule your default flow to resume afterward, or the temporary one will keep running.


##


**Let emergencies reach you, day or night**


The menu fix covered the workday, but after business hours, even an urgent call still went straight to voicemail. Sidrah added an option to the after-hours menu for customers who need assistance right away. It rings her, and if she misses it, Sona takes the call, finds out what’s wrong, and sends the team a summary so Sidrah can call the customer back.


“We get that summary right away, and I’ll hop on calling the customer back,” she said.


The menu’s other options send callers to Sona or straight to voicemail. Sona introduces itself as Maid In T.O.’s virtual assistant, answers questions about services and prices, and texts the booking link; then the team calls back the next day. Quo transcribes voicemails so the team can follow up on those, too.


### **How to set up an after-hours phone menu in Quo:**


1. In the call flow builder, drag a **Phone menu** step onto the **After hours** path of your **Business hours** step.
2. Click **Add greeting message** and click
3. **Add keypad option** for each choice.
4. Add a voice-triggered keyword option that callers can say to select a specific menu option.
5. Add a Sona step first and set its voice under **Personality** and greeting — for example, “This is Sona, Maid In T.O.’s virtual assistant.” For more, see[Sona setup and configuration](https://support.quo.com/core-concepts/ai-automations/sona/overview) .
6. In the Sona step’s **Jobs** section, click **Add job** , start from the message-taking template, and add what Sona should find out from urgent callers, such as what’s wrong.
7. Set the urgent option’s destination to **Ring users** , choosing the owner or whoever is on call. Check the ring duration so Sona doesn’t pick up before you can answer.
8. Below it, add a **Go to** step and choose your Sona step, so unanswered calls go to Sona. **Go to** can only point at a step that already exists, so build Sona first.
9. Set another option’s destination to Sona and the last to **Voicemail** . Turn on **Transcribe voicemail** . Sona answers pricing questions and texts the booking link once you set up its knowledge and a job.
10. Click **Publish** . Then click **Calls** at the top of your inbox to read the AI summary of each call Sona handled.


##


**Let Sona quote the job before asking for details**


What Sona says on those calls comes from its knowledge, which Sidrah called its training manual. It holds Maid In T.O.’s full pricing, organized by number of bedrooms and square footage, plus add-ons like baseboards and windows. Sona now asks callers only what it needs to price the job, including which add-ons they want. It then puts together a package, gives the breakdown, and sends the booking link so callers can book online or call back. The team follows up for the rest.


Early on, Sona also asked callers for their home address, which was where they dropped off. Sidrah’s read was that people don’t want to hand over an address before they’ve spoken to a human. “Customers would just go blank,” she said.


She changed Sona’s instructions to ask only for the general area, nearest intersection, or postal code. Sona would then tell callers the team would follow up or they could book through the link. Callers started talking with Sona more, she said.


### **How to teach Sona your prices in Quo:**


1. In the call flow builder, select your **Sona** step.
2. In the **Knowledge** section, click **Add knowledge** , then add your website URL, upload a pricing file (PDF, CSV, Markdown, JSON, or plain text, up to 10 MB), or type or paste in your prices and add-ons. Pages max out at 20,000 characters, so keep pricing on its own page. For example, Maid In T.O.’s pricing is organized by bedrooms, square footage, and add-ons.
3. In the **Jobs** section, click **Add job** and start from the **Scheduling** template.
4. In the instructions, name the goal first, number your steps, and list what Sona should collect. If you quote add-ons, tell Sona to ask about them and put together a package from your pricing. Ask for a postal code or nearest intersection instead of a full address. For example, you could add this line to the job’s instructions: “Ask for the caller’s postal code or nearest intersection, not their full address. Let them know the team will follow up, or they can book with the link.”
5. Tell Sona to ask whether the caller wants a text before sending one. Type a forward slash (/) to add actions to the instructions and choose **Send SMS** , then add your booking link and opt-out language, such as “Reply STOP to unsubscribe.” **Send SMS** only works on[numbers registered for business messaging](https://support.quo.com/getting-started/carrier-registration/carrier-registration) . It texts the person on the call, not a teammate or any other number.
6. Click **Optimize** to rewrite your instructions so Sona follows them more reliably, or click **Undo** to go back.
7. Click **Test Sona** and place a test call. Check your inbox for the text. Then click **Publish** . If you edit something Sona already has, like updating a price, it uses the new version right away. If you add something new or take something away, nothing changes until you click **Publish** .
8. Review call summaries regularly to spot questions Sona couldn’t answer, and update its knowledge.


##


**Start adjusting your own call flow with Quo**


Sidrah said the team is “constantly tweaking” its call flow to serve callers better. Holiday call flows are next, and Quo can[schedule them ahead of time](https://support.quo.com/core-concepts/administration/call-flows/temp-call-flows) . “I can’t wait to get to work with all the advanced options now,” she said.


Want to find out where your callers drop off? Start with the **Home services estimate** and **Business hours with Sona**[call flow templates](http://quo.com/templates) . Our[home services call flows guide](https://support.quo.com/core-concepts/administration/call-flows/guides/home-services-call-flows) covers ring groups, after-hours routing, and more.
